conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; your honest feelings help us figure out the best support for you. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you give permission to share or there’s an urgent safety concern. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… I can still laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. Maybe once or twice I’ve chuckled at something my husband said, but mostly I feel too tired to find things funny right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can laugh, but it feels kind of forced. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video, yet the laughter doesn’t feel as light or natural as it used to—more like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it bubbles up on its own.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when I think about taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but they’re pretty faint. Most of the time I’m just focused on getting through the next feeding or diaper change, so the enjoyment feels kind of muted or far away.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking, “Maybe I’m not reading her cues right,” or, “I must be doing something wrong.” I know, logically, that babies just fuss, but the little voice in my head still jumps straight to “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly I’m worried about her—like whether she’s eating enough or if that tiny cough means something serious. It’s not totally “no good reason,” but the thoughts spin in my head even when everything looks fine. I’ll check her breathing three times a night even though she’s never had any problems.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full-on panic, but a couple of times, when she’s crying and I can’t figure out what she needs, my chest gets tight and my thoughts start racing—like, “What if I can’t calm her? What if something’s really wrong?" It passes once she settles, but in the moment it feels scary and out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up and I haven’t even brushed my teeth, it feels like I’m drowning a little. I usually get through it, but it’s overwhelming more often than I’d like to admit—like I’m always one step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not really that I’m unhappy-happy, more just keyed-up and tense. After her two-o’clock feed my mind keeps running through the day—“Did I sterilize the bottles right? Is she gaining enough weight?”—so it takes me a long time to drift off again. A few nights a week I lie there an hour or more before I finally sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some days, but it comes and goes. Like yesterday afternoon, I was rocking her and suddenly felt this wave of “Is this my life now?” and my eyes got watery. It’s not all day, every day—more like clouds drifting in and out.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I actually haven’t cried much—maybe once last week when she wouldn’t latch and I felt completely useless. Mostly the tears stay stuck behind my eyes; they don’t spill over, but the ache is still there.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

You've shared that the joy and spontaneity you once felt has dimmed since your baby arrived: laughter feels forced, excitement is only a faint spark, and waves of sadness drift in unexpectedly. You often blame yourself when your daughter fusses, lie awake running through worries about her health, and sometimes feel overwhelmed or panicky when you can't soothe her right away. These feelings come and go, but they're real, heavy, and different from the "you" you remember.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and spontaneity of laughter, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only faint sparks of enjoyment, much less than before, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive worries about baby's health that override reassurance, occurring nightly—matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden chest tightness and racing thoughts triggered by baby's crying, fitting "Yes, sometimes" for unexpected panic symptoms.</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent overwhelm ('some days, yeah...drowning a little...one step behind') matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent sadness that is noticeable and emotionally impactful, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 17 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse core symptoms: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), persistent self-reproach, recurrent worry, and episodic chest tightness/racing thoughts (<sym>panic</sym>). These symptoms began post-delivery, fluctuate but impair daily and nighttime functioning, and align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Because EPDS is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, urgent clinical evaluation is recommended to confirm diagnosis and plan care. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full assessment and treatment planning
2. Continue regular contact with your maternity care team; bring this EPDS result to your next visit
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline, both compatible with breastfeeding
4. Involve trusted family/friends for practical help-meals, laundry, night-time baby care-to protect your sleep
5. Practice 10 minutes of paced breathing or gentle stretching when the baby sleeps; pair with outdoor stroller walks for light and movement
6. Keep a brief mood log; note any worsening thoughts, safety concerns, or inability to function and seek help immediately
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with follow-up clarification

Symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate intensity)
- Anhedonia: laughter feels forced; enjoyment “muted/far away” (Items 1, 2)
- Depressed mood: intermittent waves of sadness, tearfulness (Item 8); near-crying when feeding difficulties occur (Item 9)
- Guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to maternal failure (Item 3)
- Excessive anxiety: repetitive worries about infant’s health/safety, nocturnal checking, racing thoughts after feeds (Items 4, 7)
- Panic-like episodes: chest tightness, racing thoughts when unable to soothe infant (Item 5)
- Feeling overwhelmed: “drowning,” chronically behind tasks (Item 6)
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating (Item 7)

Denies thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant (Item 10)

Pattern: Symptoms began post-delivery, fluctuate in intensity, interfere with sleep and daily functioning; no current safety concern.

Screening impression: elevated risk for perinatal depression and anxiety; score range consistent with “probable minor–moderate PPD.” Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS/PHQ-9/GAAD) and psychosocial evaluation; parent support and sleep-hygiene education; routine safety re-screen at next contact.
